NB I’ve developed this map more practically in the rest of the method, which is why I’m comfortable publishing this provisional synthesis (parts of which are directly research based, the whole of which is my own):

i) child on her own – orientation and external safety

ii) child with borrowed adult – experience of at least one good adult function, personified by a real/remembered/imagined/symbolic figure

iii) adult as apprentice – with help, adult tries to do at least one part of looking after the child

iv) adult in her own right – adult repeats as many times as necessary, to build up the capacity to summon it at will: offering the child warmth, protection and direction

v) adult in relation to child – adult in charge but not banishing child, child no longer solely responsible for managing life

The child doesn’t need to stop being a child – you just become bigger than the child-state. A useful saying to yourself might be: ‘I don’t need to stop being this child, but I am also becoming an adult…’

Monogamy, particularly the sexual aspect of it, has become much more important since agriculture, and the advent of property and inheritance. response.text:
Make the Protector Visible

Protecting your little ones are you setting boundaries? When the little one feels lonely and wants to text his ex who dumped him via text at 2am in the morning, can he rely on you to put the phone in another room so that in the morning it is easier for him to be able to believe your words that you are glad he is there with you?

Most of the time your actions as a protector are seen by the little one. Every time you set a boundary or say no to something that you know would be bad for the little one, you are building trust. Dealing with those letters from the bank, keeping a promise, cleaning your room – these things demonstrate your trustworthiness to your little one. If you try to soothe your little one but don’t then do what you said you would do, to the little one it feels like the unreliable people from their past. Leaving a degrading relationship is also a protector thing!

Other protecting activities are carried out in your head. Stopping yourself from acting on fear, rage, cravings, shame etc in terms of what you say, send, buy, take, do, have sex with, commit to etc. This often involves not acting right away when you feel like you don’t have time. These actions are between you and the little one. Allowing the little one to be sarcastic with you without retaliating is a good example. Or letting the little one not to trust you without trying to convince him otherwise.

The little one may grumble that you only turn up when things are bad but, yes, that is what you do and letting him know that is also a good thing. Calling yourself an idiot to yourself and then going back to the little one to say sorry is another. All of these things are seen by the little one. Not retaliating shows him that despite what he may believe, you do love him. If your nurturer isn’t in the picture yet, you as the protector can start to build a relationship with the little one. It may take a while to develop the nurturing side but you can start.

Choose one thing to do and work out when you are going to do it. Make it small and easy if you need to. Work out whether you need any help to do it. Rehearse the difficult bits in your mind before hand. If you are saying no to someone, it is often difficult in the pause after you’ve said no but before they have replied.

Once you have done it, review whether it helped. If you haven’t experienced any relief it doesn’t mean that it didn’t help or that it was a failure. Keep doing the things that help you feel more safe, more connected, more able and/or help you enjoy life more. If they don’t, stop doing them. If you haven’t done what you said you would, work out why. Was it fear? Or did you decide it wasn’t something you wanted to achieve? Or didn’t you know how? Were you too tired? Or the office was shut?

response.text:
Building Trust With Your Little One

Keep Your Word

It’s okay if you don’t feel love or any other warm fuzzy feeling for your little one yet. The Protector can do these things first and the feelings may come later.

Choose one. Be specific about what you’re going to do, when you’re going to do it, what the first step is, and what you need to help you to do it. If there’s anything you need to practice in order to say or do, practice it. After you’ve had a chance to try it out, debrief with yourself about what happened. If you didn’t do what you said you were going to do, ask yourself if you were afraid, if you didn’t know what you were aiming for, if you didn’t know how to do it, if you were too tired or if there was some other practical problem. If you did what you said you were going to do but didn’t feel any better, recognize that just because you did it doesn’t mean that it was helpful. On the other hand, if it helped your little one to be safe, close, competent, or happy, keep doing it.

Either way, you may have skipped over some of the above, and believe you’re ready to venture out and meet your little guy…guy? gal? it? Whoever or whatever it is, your little buddy probably should stay put for now.

response.text:
If you can’t come up with anything, do this exercise for your Protector. I’m sure he or she can think of a few things that they do to take care of little one. They lock the door at night, or make sure little one eats, or say no to social occasions so little one can have a good night’s rest, or put the phone away when it rings at midnight. The warm fuzzy feelings will come later.

Choose one thing from the list to do. Make it specific – you will do ____ at ____ time. What is the first thing you need to do? Who can help you? It may be useful to rehearse what you will say, and debrief afterwards about how it went. If you didn’t do the thing, ask yourself what got in the way – were you afraid? Did you not know what you wanted to do? Did you not know how to do it? Were you too tired? Was something getting in the way? If you did do the thing, notice whether or not you feel better afterwards. It may be that even though you did the thing you are supposed to do to make little one safe/closeness/competent/happy, little one doesn’t actually feel safe/close/competent/happy. Only do things which are helpful.

response.text: Then, once you’ve done it (or not!) you can then see what happened, and how it made you feel. It’s important to remember that if you didn’t feel any better after doing it, that doesn’t mean it was a waste of time. And if you did feel better, that doesn’t mean you should always do that thing. Maybe it’s something you need to do to keep you safe, or be close to someone, or help you do something you like, or get better at something – most of the time you can just tick it off. And if you didn’t do the thing, that doesn’t mean anything either. Maybe you didn’t feel you could do it, or you didn’t want to do it in the end, or you didn’t know how to do it, or you were too tired, or the friend you thought you could ask to help you didn’t reply.
